title: Large Language Model Steering of Acousto-Optic Tweezer Arrays
authors: Cheng Sheng, Kai-xuan Xiao, Yin Zhang, Wen-hao Wang, Feng-yi Zhang, Xu-xing Geng, Guang-ming Huang, Gao-xiang Li
abstract: Controlling quantum hardware requires choosing and revising experimental strategies as nonlinear response, coupling, and drift limit calibration. We experimentally investigate a general-purpose large language model (LLM) as a human-in-the-loop strategy layer for a neutral-atom tweezer platform. Through step-by-step interaction with experimental feedback, the LLM guides a transition from multiplicative row--column correction to a drift-corrected local response-matrix method when separable feedback stalls. Deterministic software performs image analysis and numerical updates, while an experimentalist verifies and authorizes each waveform. For a $10\times10$ crossed-acousto-optic-deflector array, this workflow reduces the Gaussian-peak coefficient of variation from $20.30\%$ to $1.57\%$ in 30 candidate-update rounds. The experiment demonstrates feedback-informed strategy selection on a physical quantum-control subsystem, rather than direct generation of control parameters alone. These results highlight the potential of LLMs to guide control optimization across diverse quantum platforms by adaptively formulating and refining experimental strategies.
summary: The research demonstrates using a Large Language Model (LLM) as an intelligent, human-in-the-loop layer to guide the complex calibration of acousto-optic tweezer arrays for neutral atoms. By adaptively selecting and refining control strategies—such as switching from simple to local response matrix fitting—the system achieved a significant reduction in spatial intensity variation. This highlights a powerful paradigm for using AI to manage the iterative, expert-driven optimization of quantum control systems.
main_problem: Controlling quantum hardware, specifically neutral-atom tweezer arrays, requires adapting experimental strategies to compensate for nonlinear responses, coupling, and drift.
main_result: An LLM-guided workflow successfully optimized the tweezer array control, reducing the Gaussian-peak coefficient of variation from 20.30% to 1.57% over 30 update rounds.
method: The study uses a human-in-the-loop approach where an LLM guides the selection and refinement of control models, transitioning from simple row-column corrections to a complex local response-matrix method.
model_or_system: The physical system is a neutral-atom tweezer platform utilizing a $10 	imes 10$ crossed-acousto-optic-deflector (AOD) array to trap and manipulate atoms.
key_observables: Gaussian-peak coefficient of variation (CV), diffraction efficiency, and optical intensities measured on a feedback CCD.
important_parameters: The optimization involves characterizing the RF-to-optical response using multiple tones and minimizing a Tikhonov objective function related to the local response matrix.
main_assumptions: The LLM's utility is demonstrated in guiding strategy selection rather than directly generating optimal control parameters, and the minimum CV is noted as the best observed value.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the LLM-guided optical control loop, showing the setup, measured intensity arrays, and the step-by-step optimization trajectory tracking the CV reduction across different control strategies.
paper_structure: The paper details the necessity of adaptive control, presents the LLM-guided workflow, shows the mathematical transition between control models (row-column to local MIMO), and quantifies the performance improvement via CV reduction over iterative rounds.
why_interesting: This work bridges advanced quantum control theory with modern AI tools, showing how LLMs can manage the complex, multi-stage decision-making process inherent in optimizing physical quantum hardware.
